title: Tenant Ebb-Flow Capacity Controller — PRD sketch
body:
Summary:

This doc sketches a new controller for Dedicated pools that treats capacity as an ebb-and-flow system: tenants have steady-state allocations (the reef) plus transient surge allowances (the tidal band). The goal is to provide predictable baseline latency + cost while enabling short-term bursts with bounded impact to co-tenants. This is an API + policy + runtime design that slots between the reservation ledger and the runtime scheduler.

Motivation / Problem statement:
- Many tenants have spiky UX-driven workloads (search, chat sessions, batch embedding spikes) that are inefficient to overprovision for.
- Current burst mechanisms either (a) allow unlimited opportunistic use (noisy neighbors), or (b) gate bursts too aggressively (customer frustration).
- We need a system that: minimizes baseline overcommit, provides short burst elasticity, enforces isolation during extended surges, and makes economics transparent to customers and SRE.

High-level goals:
- Fast, few-second bursts for tail-latency-sensitive requests with predictable degradation behavior if bursts continue.
- Soft accounting: tenants can accumulate or borrow burst credits with decay windows (ebb/flow).
- Fairness: ensure tenants cannot monopolize spare capacity for long windows; prefer recent idle pools for bursts.
- Observable: per-tenant credit balances, burst history, and explainable throttles in Console.

Non-goals:
- This is not a full replacement for Reserved Capacity contracts or the long-lived Dedicated reservations marketplace.
- Not addressing multi-region failover in this iteration.

Design overview:
- Reef (steady state): right-sized baseline reservation (existing reserved capacity).
- Tidal band (burst capacity): time-limited pool of opportunistic capacity carved from underutilized hosts or pre-warmed ephemeral instances.
- Credit engine: each tenant has a credit balance based on historical utilization vs commitment. Credits accumulate slowly when under baseline and are spent when bursting. Credits decay with a configurable half-life.
- Surge governor: runtime admission control that uses credits + instantaneous queue depth + per-tenant SLO weight to admit or reject burst requests.

Controller behavior (runtime steps):
1) Request arrives -> route -> candidate serving pool selected (reef + tidal sources).
2) If reef has headroom -> serve with baseline SLO.
3) If reef saturated -> consult credit engine: if tenant has credits > threshold and tidal pool has available slots -> allow burst.
4) When admitted to tidal pool the tenant incurs a credit burn and a short-lived affinity (soft pin) to the ephemeral slot to reduce cold-starts for immediate follow-ups.
5) If bursts persist and credits expire -> degrade to graceful throttles or fallback to a cheaper model variant (quality-latency tradeoff).

Credit model (sketch):
- Earn rate = f(commitment utilization delta) — e.g., tenants earn credits when using <70% of committed baseline.
- Spend rate = proportional to burst time and observed per-second token consumption.
- Cap: credits are capped (e.g., 24h of baseline throughput) to prevent long offline accumulation abuse.
- Decay: credits decay with configurable window (default 48h half-life) to keep market fluid.

Tidal pool sizing and sourcing:
- Primary source: hosts in Dedicated fleet with low utilization (opportunistic slices) + short-lived pre-warmed nodes.
- Safety margin: always maintain a minimum headroom (10-15% of total fleet) for critical SLO preservation.
- Admission policy: per-tenant admission is weighted by credit and SLO tier (enterprise customers with higher tier get higher admission weight).

Isolation controls and QoS:
- Soft-fencing: when tidal consumption exceeds thresholds, reduce per-tenant burst ratios proportionally (no absolute evictions unless thresholds hit).
- Hard-fencing: automated circuit-breaker that enforces strict burst caps for tenants that exceed sustained surplus for X minutes.
- Graceful degradation: policy to swap to smaller/quantized model or synthetic rate-limit headers to clients with explicit reason codes for observability.

APIs and Console surface:
- New REST endpoints for: get_credit_balance, simulate_burst(cost_estimate), request_tidal_reserve, release_affinity.
- Console widgets: per-tenant credit graph, burst events timeline, projected burn rate if current traffic continues, recommended commit uplift.

Metrics & SLOs to track:
- Mean and P95 serving latency for reef vs tidal.
- Burst admission rate and rejection rate per tenant.
- Credit balance distribution across top N tenants.
- Incidents where tidal admission caused reef SLO regressions (should be near-zero).

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (experiment): In-house A/B with small set of internal tenants; run credit model in observe-only.
- Phase 1 (beta): Opt-in for select customers (special flag), aggressive telemetry and manual kill-switch.
- Phase 2 (GA): Global rollout with default conservative limits and self-serve controls.

Operational playbook snippets (ops notes):
- If reef SLOs degrade: throttle tidal admission globally, increase safety margin, and notify on-call.
- For billing disputes: provide credit timeline + request trace + alternative model fallback evidence.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Economic model: Should bursts be priced at premium token rate or buffered into committed tiers? Mixed models have behavioral effects.
- Complexity: how much of the credit math should be customer-visible vs internal tuning?
- Fairness across different workload shapes (steady low qps vs spiky high token-per-request).

Next steps / tasks:
- Engineering spike: simulator to validate credit model under synthetic mixes (done by infra/ops).
- UX: Console mockups for credit controls and explainability.
- Legal/Billing: proposal for burst pricing and dispute flows.
- Runbook: concrete commands for SRE to throttle tidal and to backfill reservations.

Appendix: quick sim notes (sketch)
- Sim parameters: 100 tenants, mix of 70% low-burst, 20% medium, 10% high. Tidal pool = 12% of capacity. Credit decay = 48h half-life.
- Early result (sim): median P95 latency preserved with 1.8x reduction in committed capacity needs for mixed workloads.

Notes to self and team: this is intentionally a hybrid metaphor (reef/tidal) to help product explainability. Need to iterate metric thresholds (safety margin, earn/spend multipliers) with SRE and pricing with finance. Will add sequence diagrams and API spec next draft.
